app.title: Openstring — guitar reading trainer that listens
chords.hadErrors: Got there, but not first time.
chords.prompt: Press start, then play the chord you see.
chords.readIntro: Several notes at once on the staff. Play them one string at a time, from the lowest upward — that is how you check you have really fingered the chord, and it is the only way the microphone can hear whether each note is right.
chords.shapesIntro: Pick a chord and see where the fingers go. × means do not play that string, ○ means play it open, and the numbers are which finger.
chords.waiting: Play it from the lowest string up.
chords.wrongNote: Not that one — try it again.
data.backupNudge: You have a few weeks of practice saved here and no backup. Clearing your browser data would erase it. Export takes one click.
data.eraseConfirm: Erase all progress on this machine? This cannot be undone.
data.heading: Your data
data.importFailed: That file could not be read: {message}
data.intro: Everything lives in this browser only. Nothing is uploaded anywhere. Export it if you want a backup or want to move machines.
data.storageBlocked: This browser is not letting the page save anything, so your progress will vanish when you close the tab. Private browsing usually causes this.
grade.aheadBy: ahead of the beat by {ms} ms
grade.colourVaried: tone varied by {factor}x across the phrase
grade.shapeMissing: the loud and soft did not really happen
grade.uneven: some notes much louder than others
lang.helpTranslate: Spot a clumsy phrase? Corrections are welcome on GitHub.
lang.label: Language
lesson.backToTheNote: Leave this for now and go back to the note on its own. It will be easier when you come back.
lesson.hearItFirst: Have a listen first — press “Play it for me”, then try it.
lesson.l1.advice: Do not spell your way up from the bottom line. Look at where the note sits and recognise it. That recognition, not counting, is what reading is.
lesson.l1.blurb: Two notes, and neither needs a finger. G sits on the second line — the one the treble clef curls around, which is why it is called the G clef. B is the middle line. Two lines, two open strings, and by the end of this you will have played a duet.
lesson.l1.title: Two lines
lesson.l10.advice: Second finger for E, third for F. Same two fingers, same two frets, every bass string from here on — learn the shape once and the rest is bookkeeping.
lesson.l10.blurb: E and F on the fourth string, second and third frets. Two at once because it is one hand shape, and it is the same shape you will use on the fifth and sixth strings next.
lesson.l10.title: Fingers on the fourth
lesson.l11.advice: If this felt easier than the fourth string did, that is the point. The shape is the same; only the names changed.
lesson.l11.blurb: B and C on the fifth string. The same shape as last time, one string down — which is the first moment the neck starts to feel like a system rather than a list.
lesson.l11.title: Fingers on the fifth
lesson.l12.advice: First finger for F, third for G — a different pair from the last two lessons, because the gap here is two frets rather than one. Look at the fretboard picture before you assume.
lesson.l12.blurb: F and G on the lowest string, first and third frets. The last two notes of open position, and after them there is nothing left to add.
lesson.l12.title: Fingers on the sixth
lesson.l13.advice: If a note is slow here it is almost never the pitch — it is the string you are unsure of. Notice which one it is and that is your practice for the week.
lesson.l13.blurb: Nothing new. Seventeen notes, all six strings, everything you have learned mixed together — and the run to finish it is twenty in a row rather than ten, because this is the end of open position and it should feel like it.
lesson.l13.title: The whole open position
lesson.l2.advice: Three landmarks is deliberately few. They are anchors, not a scale — the point is that you never count lines again, you measure from the nearest one you know.
lesson.l2.blurb: E, the thinnest string, in the top space just under the highest line. That is the third landmark, and with it every other note on the guitar can be found by stepping from whichever of the three is nearest.
lesson.l2.title: The top space
lesson.l3.advice: Keep the finger close behind the fret, not on the wire. A buzz is almost always the finger sitting on top of the fret rather than behind it.
lesson.l3.blurb: The first note you actually finger: A, second fret of the third string. One note is not a small ambition — it is exactly what a method book gives you after the open strings, and four notes is already enough for a tune everybody knows.
lesson.l3.title: Two frets along
lesson.l4.advice: First finger for C. Leave it there while you play the open strings around it — a hand that resets between every note is a hand that will never get fast.
lesson.l4.blurb: C, the first fret of the second string. Four notes become five, and one of the most famous four-note figures ever written is now under your hand.
lesson.l4.title: One step higher
lesson.l5.advice: Third finger for D, first for C, and the hand stays put. This is also the first lesson with a dotted rhythm, so count it out loud before you play it.
lesson.l5.blurb: D, the third fret of the second string. Five notes, and the folk repertoire opens up properly — three of the pieces here are tunes you already know by heart.
lesson.l5.title: The five-note world
lesson.l6.advice: Check you are on the first string and not the second. F and the open E are one fret apart, which is why they get confused, and why hearing the difference matters more here than anywhere so far.
lesson.l6.blurb: F, the first fret of the thinnest string. It is a half step above E — the smallest distance on the instrument, and the one most often played by accident.
lesson.l6.title: The first fret
lesson.l7.advice: Two Gs, one at each end. Play them one after the other and listen: that sameness is what an octave is, and hearing it is worth more than being told it.
lesson.l7.blurb: G at the third fret of the first string — the same letter as the G you started on, an octave up. The top three strings are now complete and a tune can go anywhere on them.
lesson.l7.title: The octave closed
lesson.l8.advice: Expect to be slower down here at first. Notes below the staff are counted from a line that is not printed until the note needs it, so they take longer to recognise. That is normal and it wears off.
lesson.l8.blurb: D, the open fourth string — and the first note that will not fit on the staff at all. It gets its own short line underneath, a ledger line, and everything below the staff works that way.
lesson.l8.title: Below the staff
lesson.l9.advice: The low E is the hardest note for the app to hear and the easiest to play badly. Pluck it cleanly rather than hard; a thick string played hard goes sharp before it settles.
lesson.l9.blurb: The last two open strings, A and the low E. Two at once because they are one skill — no fingers, both below the staff, and the lowest notes the guitar has.
lesson.l9.title: The floor of the instrument
lesson.mapIntro: Every lesson, in order. You can go back to any lesson you have already reached.
lesson.slowItDown: This is too fast to think at. Take the tempo down and get it right slowly.
lesson.step.duet: Duet: “{title}” — the app plays the other part
lesson.step.ear: Learn “{title}” by ear, before you can read it
lesson.step.rhythm: Play the rhythm against the click
lesson.step.warmup: Warm up on the notes you already know
lesson.tryAgain: Not that one. Have another go.
library.heading: Music you can play now
library.intro: Short pieces and duets built only from notes you have already met. On a duet the app plays the other part.
library.none: Finish the first lesson and the music appears here.
mic.refused: Microphone permission was refused. Allow it in your browser settings and reload.
piece.chunksIntro: Seams are the joins between chunks. They get extra attention because that is where pieces come apart.
piece.cleanAgain: Clean — once more at this tempo
piece.heading: Practise a piece
piece.intro: Bring in a piece as MusicXML — Guitar Pro and MuseScore both export it (File → Export → MusicXML, uncompressed .musicxml or .xml). Openstring splits it into short chunks, drills each one, then drills the joins between them, raising the tempo only when you play it clean.
piece.mxlHint: (If you exported a compressed .mxl, re-export as uncompressed MusicXML.)
piece.noNotes: That score has no playable notes.
piece.octave.assumed: This file has no fingering and declares no transposition, so the pitches were taken as what the guitar sounds. If every note comes out an octave wrong, flip the octave switch.
piece.octave.builtIn: Built in, and fingered for exactly the notes this lesson has taught.
piece.octave.inconsistent: This file mixes both octave conventions. Check a few notes before trusting it.
piece.octave.sounding: Pitches match the string and fret positions exactly, so they are sounding pitch.
piece.octave.transpose: Used the transposition declared in the file.
piece.octave.unverified: The fingering in this file does not agree with its own pitches, so the octave could not be confirmed. Assuming the pitches are what the guitar sounds.
piece.octave.written: Pitches sit an octave above the string and fret positions, so they are written pitch.
piece.playAfterCountIn: Press start, then play it after the count-in.
piece.playedItAnyway: You got to the end. That is the thing that matters today.
piece.playedItThrough: That was the whole piece, clean.
piece.playingThrough: Playing it through — keep going to the end.
piece.removeConfirm: Remove this piece and its practice history?
progress.finishedPlan: You have finished the whole plan. Keep the last stage running to stay sharp.
progress.fluentRatio: {fluent} of {total} notes are fast and accurate
progress.heatIntro: Green is fast and accurate. Amber is correct but slow — that is not learned yet. Red needs work. Grey has not come up yet. Dashed means it is not part of this stage.
progress.notEnoughAttempts: not every note has been asked enough times yet
progress.weakEmpty: Nothing yet — play a session first.
progress.weakNone: Nothing is lagging behind. Either you are doing well or you have not played much yet.
read.endedIdle: Session ended — nothing played for a few minutes.
read.goalHintPractice: A practice round. A level is finished by a run without slips.
read.goalHintStreak: One slip and the count starts again.
read.goalNextRound: Takes effect on the next round.
read.openString: That is the {string} string open — right string, no finger down.
read.outOfTune: The {name} string sounds out of tune. Tap here to check it — a note played on a string that is out is heard as a different note.
read.prompt: Press start, then play the note you see.
read.sessionDone: Session done — {correct} of {asked} right first time.
read.stageComplete: Stage complete — you have these. Next: {next}.
rhythm.accuracyBody: Your computer adds a small, unknown delay between the string moving and the browser hearing it. That means consistency — whether your notes are evenly spaced — is always measured correctly, but rushing or dragging is only as accurate as the delay estimate below. Headphones are strongly recommended: through speakers the microphone hears the click itself and counts it as a note.
rhythm.countIn: One bar of count-in, then play.
rhythm.dragging: Dragging — you are behind the click
rhythm.heading: Play the rhythm against the click
rhythm.intro: This is the half most free tools skip. Pitch does not matter here — play any note, or tap the body of the guitar. What is measured is when.
rhythm.nothingHeardWhy: Check the microphone is picking you up — the level bar on the Read tab should move when you play.
rhythm.rushing: Rushing — you are ahead of the click
rhythm.uneven: Uneven — no steady bias, just scattered
stage.first-twelve.advice: From here on, reading is about choosing the most comfortable place, not finding the only one.
stage.first-twelve.blurb: The whole neck up to the octave, naturals and accidentals. The same pitch now lives in several places and you choose.
stage.first-twelve.title: The first twelve frets
stage.landmarks.advice: Do not spell your way up from the bottom line. Look at where the note sits and ask first whether it is one of these three — that recognition, not counting, is what reading is.
stage.landmarks.blurb: Three notes only, and all three are open strings — nothing to finger. G sits on the second line, the one the clef curls around. B is the middle line. E is the top space, just under the highest line. Learn where these three are and every other note can be found by stepping from the nearest one.
stage.landmarks.title: Three landmarks
stage.open-bass.advice: Ledger lines are just the staff continuing past its own edge. Count down from the bottom line rather than trying to recognise them whole.
stage.open-bass.blurb: Three notes again, and again nothing to finger: the open D, A and low E. They sit below the staff on ledger lines, which is the only thing that is new about them.
stage.open-bass.title: The three bass strings, open
stage.open-bottom.advice: These notes sit low on the staff and need ledger lines. Expect to be slower here than on the top strings at first.
stage.open-bottom.blurb: The frets on the bass strings now: six new notes joining the three open ones you have. That is the whole of open position, all six strings, naturals only.
stage.open-bottom.title: Open position, bottom three strings
stage.open-chromatic.advice: An accidental changes the name, not the line it sits on. F and F sharp live on the same line.
stage.open-chromatic.blurb: The same region, now including the notes between. Same places on the neck, more names to attach.
stage.open-chromatic.title: Open position with sharps and flats
stage.open-top.advice: Say each note name out loud as you play it. Out loud matters — it forces the name and the place to arrive together. When a note is unfamiliar, find the landmark nearest it and step from there.
stage.open-top.blurb: Two last notes: F and G on the first string — E there is already a landmark. The first string repeats the shape you just learned on the second: open, first fret, third fret. That completes an octave, G up to G, with nothing left over.
stage.open-top.title: Open position, top three strings
stage.position-v.advice: Nothing is open here, so your hand has no anchor. That is the point — this is where the neck starts to generalise.
stage.position-v.blurb: Frets five to eight, all six strings. The first shift away from the open strings.
stage.position-v.title: Fifth position
stage.string-3.advice: A is the next letter up from G, so on the staff it sits in the space directly above the line G lives on. One step up the page, two frets along the string.
stage.string-3.blurb: One new note. G is already yours — the open third string, the first of your landmarks. A sits two frets along the same string, and that is the whole stage.
stage.string-3.title: The third string
stage.strings-23.advice: Watch the shape. On the second string the notes fall on the open string, the first fret and the third. The first string uses exactly the same shape, so learning it here makes the next stage half free.
stage.strings-23.blurb: Two new notes, C and D, both on the second string — B there is already a landmark. Five notes now, across two strings.
stage.strings-23.title: Second and third strings
sync.chooseDirection: Signed in. Nothing has been changed — this device already has practice on it, so choose whether to send it up or bring the stored progress down.
sync.expired: Your sign-in has expired. Sign in again.
sync.heading: Sync across your devices
sync.intro: Optional. Sign in with your email and your progress follows you to your phone or another computer. No password — you get a link by email. Nothing you play is ever uploaded, only the numbers.
sync.pullConfirm: Replace this device's progress with what is stored? Anything practised here and not yet sent up will be lost.
sync.pushConfirm: Replace what is stored for your account with this device's progress? Anything practised on another device and not yet brought down will be lost.
sync.pushed: Sent. This device is now the copy of record.
sync.sendFailed: Could not send the sign-in email.
sync.signedIn: Signed in. Progress brought down from the server.
tools.metroIntro: Works on its own — no microphone needed.
tools.pinnedHint: Tuning string {string} only. Tap it again to let the tuner choose.
tools.pressStart: Press start, then play a string.
tools.stringsHint: Tap a string to tune only that one. A tick means it held in tune for half a second.
tools.tapHint: Tap four times in time to set the tempo.
tools.tunerIntro: Play one string at a time. It works out which string you are on, stays on it, and tells you which way to turn the peg.
welcome.heading: Learn to read music on the guitar
welcome.lede: A note appears on the staff. You play it. Openstring listens and tells you whether you found it, how long you took, and what to work on next.
welcome.needGuitarWhy: Acoustic, classical or electric. Roughly in tune — there is a tuner built in.
welcome.needMicWhy: Your laptop's built-in one is fine. The browser will ask permission in a moment.
welcome.needPhonesWhy: Otherwise the microphone hears the metronome and counts it as you playing.
welcome.newbieBody: That is fine — start anyway. The first stage is eight notes in one octave, and it shows you where each one lives whenever you ask.
welcome.newbieHtml: Never read music before? That is fine — start anyway. The first lesson is three notes, none of which needs a finger, and it ends with you playing a duet: you play the three, the app plays everything underneath.
welcome.privacyBody: The audio is analysed in your browser and never recorded or uploaded — no recording is ever made. There is no subscription, ever. Your progress is saved in this browser; if you want it on your phone too you can sign in with an email link, and even then only the numbers travel, never the sound.
welcome.privacyHtml: Nothing you play leaves this device. The audio is analysed in your browser and never recorded or uploaded — no recording is ever made. There is no subscription, ever. Your progress is saved in this browser; if you want it on your phone too you can sign in with an email link, and even then only the numbers travel, never the sound.
welcome.privacyLead: Nothing you play leaves this device.
welcome.unsupported: This browser cannot record audio, so the listening part will not work. Try Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox — and note the page must be served over https.
